newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SWISS JEWS SLAM DEALS ON HOLOCAUST VICTIMS' WEALTH.
newsitem.headline: SWISS JEWS SLAM DEALS ON HOLOCAUST VICTIMS' WEALTH.

text.p: Swiss Jews demanded on Wednesday the return of Holocaust victims' wealth ceded to Eastern European countries under controversial post-war accords to help compensate Swiss citizens for nationalised property.

A historian who has studied the era said Switzerland paid Poland around 480,000 Swiss francs (now $382,800) and earmarked 325,000 francs for Hungary under secret deals that Jewish groups have comdemned as robbing Holocaust victims of their wealth.

"We do not agree that Switzerland should use funds stemming from Holocaust victims to make it easier for the Poles or other states to compensate Swiss for nationalised property," said the leader of Switzerland's Jewish community, Rolf Bloch.
He told Reuters it was "indefensible" to use Holocaust victims' unclaimed wealth for such an end, insisting the funds be returned to the victims' rightful heirs or charities.

"We demand...a quick determination of the facts and of the amount of the money involved and that these be given to the heirs or to the fund set up by federal decree in 1962 to distribute dormant assets to charitable organisations," he said.
"Now I think we should search more quickly because this is no longer a question of historical events, but rather of restoring Switzerland's image."

As uproar over the secret accords mounted, Swiss historian Peter Hug published a study that showed a 1949 agreement with Poland using Poles' unclaimed wealth to help settle Swiss compensation claims was not an isolated deal.

"Switzerland made similar concessions to Hungary as it had to Poland," according to Hug's report, which was submitted to the foreign ministry in September but only emerged on Wednesday, when it was published in the Neue Zuercher Zeitung newspaper.

Berne agreed in 1950 to help Budapest, which like Poland was eager to get its hands on hard currency, search for dormant Swiss assets of Hungarians who died in the war, Hug said. He put the amount of money involved at 460,500 francs.

When the government in 1973 sought parliament's approval for a compensation treaty with Hungary, he added, it did not mention a confidential annex that credited Budapest with 325,000 francs from unclaimed Holocaust accounts to be used for the payments.

In Poland's case, Switzerland gave Warsaw 16,347 francs in 1960 and another 463,955 francs in 1975 under the 1949 pact that used unclaimed wealth from dead Poles' bank accounts and life insurance policies to help pay Swiss for nationalised property.
This was less than the two million francs mentioned in other documents from the period that are now coming to light.
"Despite several Polish requests, Switzerland refused (in 1975) to give Polish authorities the names of the people originally entitled to the funds," Hug added.
"Thus even if Poland had wanted to, it would have been impossible to identify and pay survivors entitled to the funds."
Switzerland has struggled to deal with a drumbeat of criticism from Jewish groups and a U.S. senator about the way it handled dormant accounts from Holocaust victims.

Worried that Switzerland's reputation was at a nadir, the head of parliament's foreign affairs committee this week urged the government to act more decisively and stop just reacting to a stream of damaging documents now emerging from archives.
Switzerland is tracking down dormant accounts in three ways.

A banking ombudsman is coordinating nearly 1,000 claims that have been submitted and an independent panel set up by Jewish groups and Swiss bankers will also comb banks' records for unclaimed wealth that may have escaped two previous sweeps.

Parliament is also set to give final approval in December to a panel of historians and experts empowered to lift strict banking secrecy and conduct a sweeping review of the era. ($1=1.2538 Swiss Franc)
